To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Crowdsourcing Homeland Security is a new approach to governance that offloads the responsibilities of surveillance onto the population, and in doing so, is able to produce a participatory citizenship.
the Texas Virtual Borderwatch is a crowdsourcing platform that uses the power of the internet to offload the costs of surveillance and security to the public.
the Texas Virtual Border Watch (Virtually Border Watch) is a web-based surveillance system that allows the public to view live footage of the U.S-Mexico border and report suspicious activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the Texas Virtual borderwatch as a new model for the governance and surveillance of the U.S. borderlands, and its implications for citizenship in the 21st Century.

how the Texas Virtual Borderwatch, as a form of Crowdsourcing homeland security, can be used to explore the relationship between Neoliberal governance and the development of participatory citizenship in the United States.

how the Texas Virtual Border Watch is a new example of a Neoliberal strategy for offloading the costs of surveillance and security onto the populace, while simultaneously redefining the relationship between citizen and state, and citizen and border.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the crowdsourcing model of the Texas Virtual borderwatch represents a new form of surveillance and governance, one in which the state is no longer the sole arbiter of security, but rather a network of participatory, interactive, and collaborative platforms that allow for the offloading of security onto the citizenry.

the Texas Virtual Borderwatch represents an example of the Neoliberal logic of governance, able to use participatory platforms to offload the costs of security and surveillance to the populace at no cost to the state.

the Texas Virtual Border Watch represents the latest in the Neoliberal movement to politicize everyday cultural practices, and in so doing, to create a new logic of security that offloads the responsibilities of surveillance to the populace, creating participatory “citizens-soldiers” of a new kind.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Texas Virtual Borderwatch represents a new form of Neoliberal governance that uses crowdsourced, participatory citizenship as a tool to offload the responsibility of security from the state and into the hands of the populace at a low cost to the state.
we seek to understand how the state uses new technologies to crowdsource security and how this affects the citizen’s role in security.

this paper is an exploration into the development of a “Neoliberal Logic of Labor and Surveillance” through the case of Crowdsourcing and the Texas Virtual Borderwatch, a network of web-based surveillance cameras that can be patroled by anyone with an Internet connection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Texas Virtual Border Watch is an important example of the way in which the state is able to use the participatory culture of the Internet to offload its responsibilities to the citizenry.
we must be aware of how these practices of surveillance and labor are not only being applied to the U.S.-Mexican border, but to the everyday lives of people around the world.

we need to understand that the state has a role in creating the very conditions for the emergence of new forms of sociality, and in doing so, the state has an interest in the reproduction of social relations.
